title: Kitchen French
intro: The words a brigade uses at the pass, from mise en place to à la minute. Say them well and the kitchen hears that you know the work behind them.

entries.title: The brigade de cuisine
entries.summary: The brigade de cuisine is the kitchen's chain of command, from the chef de cuisine down to the commis and the plongeur. It tells every cook what they own, who they answer to and how a whole kitchen moves as one.
entries.guest: In a classical kitchen the chef leads a brigade, with a sous chef as second and a cook in charge of each station, so every part of your plate has an owner.

paras: Brigade de cuisine (bree-GAHD duh kwee-ZEEN) means kitchen brigade: a team organised like a small army, where every job has one owner and every owner answers to one person. When a ticket arrives nobody wonders who is cooking the fish or making the sauce, and that clarity lets a crowded, hot kitchen work fast without collisions. For a new cook it settles the first question, who do I answer to. For a new server it explains the kitchen on the other side of the pass, the counter where finished plates leave.

The chef de cuisine (shef duh kwee-ZEEN), the head of the kitchen, sets the menu and the standards, runs the team and carries the result; chef simply means chief. The sous chef (SOO shef), the under chef, is second in command: runs the kitchen day to day, trains the cooks and takes over when the chef is away. A chef de partie (shef duh par-TEE) owns one station and the cooks on it. A demi-chef de partie is that station chef's deputy, or runs a small station alone.

The commis (koh-MEE) is a junior cook who learns one station at a time under its chef de partie. The apprenti (ah-prahn-TEE) is an apprentice, still in training. The plongeur (plohn-ZHUR), from plonger, to plunge, washes the pots, pans and plates, and without clean pans service stops within minutes. A new cook answers first to the chef de partie of the station, and goes further up the line only when sent. Going over your station chef's head breaks the very chain that keeps service calm.

The dining room, the front of house, has a brigade of its own, just as the kitchen is the back of house. The maître d'hôtel (MAY-truh doh-TEL), or maître d', runs the room. The chef de rang (shef duh RAHN) runs a section of tables, as an American captain does. The commis de rang carries plates, clears and learns the section, and the sommelier (suh-mul-YAY) looks after the wine. Between the two brigades stands the aboyeur (ah-bwah-YUR), the barker, from aboyer, to bark, who calls the orders to the stations and the plates to the waiters: the job an American kitchen calls expediting.

An American kitchen keeps the logic under plainer names: an executive chef, often over more than one kitchen, a chef de cuisine running this one, sous chefs, line cooks on the stations, prep cooks making the mise en place, the prepared ingredients, and dishwashers in the plongeur's place. The World Table borrows the ladder for its four levels, Commis, Chef de Partie, Sous Chef and Chef, each a rank earned by work, as in a kitchen.

Kitchens ran by rank long before the brigade had a name, but the system as cooks know it is credited to Auguste Escoffier (es-koff-ee-AY). He joined the hotelier César Ritz at the Savoy in London in 1890, Ritz running the hotel and Escoffier its kitchens, then set up the kitchens of the Ritz in Paris in 1898. His aim was to end duplicated effort: each station made its element for everyone, so a single plate drew on several stations working at the same moment, brought together at the pass.

Brennan's own story shows how far the ladder runs. The house records that Lazone Randolph began here as a dishwasher in 1965 and became executive chef in 2005, and that Kris Padalino, executive chef since June 2025, spent eight years in this kitchen as pastry chef and executive sous chef first. The dining room has captains; who carves, who flames and how the floor is organised on a given night are questions for lineup, the short meeting before service.

Respect for every rank is the habit of a good kitchen: please and thank you at full speed, the plongeur called by name, your own mess cleared before you leave a station. When a guest asks who cooked their dinner, the true answer is the brigade: the chef's standards, and a cook at each station who owns one part of the plate.

entries.title: The stations
entries.summary: A station, or partie, is one part of the kitchen with one job: sauces, fish, roasts, grill, fryer, vegetables, cold food, pastry. Knowing which station cooks what tells a cook where to stand and a server why a plate may be running late.
entries.guest: In a classical kitchen each part of a plate has its own station: the steak from the grill, the potatoes from the fryer, the vegetables from another cook, joined at the last moment.

paras: A station is a cook's territory: the stove, the tools, the prepared ingredients and the dishes that one cook, or one small team, owns for the night. The French word is partie, a part, which is why its leader is a chef de partie. Escoffier's brigade divided the kitchen so that every station could work at once on its own element of a plate. Learn the stations and the menu reads as a map: each dish is a set of parts, and each part has a home.

The saucier (soh-SYAY) makes the sauces and the sautéed dishes, cooked to order in a pan with their sauce. It was the senior station of the classical kitchen, because sauce was the heart of French cooking and the work leaves no margin: a reduction or a butter sauce finished at the last minute, every minute of service. In smaller kitchens the saucier usually takes the fish as well.

The poissonnier (pwah-sun-YAY) cooks the fish and seafood, and often prepares them too. The rôtisseur (roh-tee-SUR) roasts meat and poultry and makes their jus, the roasting juices served with them. The grillardin (gree-yar-DAN) works the grill and the friturier (free-too-RYAY) the fryer; in the classical scheme both work under the rôtisseur, and in a smaller kitchen the rôtisseur does both jobs.

The entremetier (ahn-truh-meh-TYAY) cooks the vegetables, soups, eggs and starches such as potatoes, rice and pasta. In the largest kitchens the job splits: a potager (poh-tah-ZHAY) makes the soups and a légumier (lay-goo-MYAY) the vegetables, both under the entremetier.

The garde manger (gard mahn-ZHAY), whose name means keeper of the food, runs the cold kitchen: salads, terrines (seasoned meat, fish or vegetable mixtures cooked in a mould and served cold), cold sauces such as mayonnaise and the cold starters. The boucher (boo-SHAY) breaks meat and poultry down into portions for the other stations. The pâtissier (pah-tee-SYAY) makes the pastry and desserts, and the boulanger (boo-lahn-ZHAY) bakes the bread. The tournant (toor-NAHN), the roundsman, covers any station on another cook's night off, so must know them all.

An American restaurant keeps the stations under plainer names along the hot line, the row of stoves, grills and fryers facing the pass. Sauté is the saucier's heir: pans, sauces and often the fish. Grill takes the steaks, chops and anything marked over the fire. Fry runs the fryers. Cold, also called pantry, plates the salads and cold starters, the garde manger's work. Pastry often works apart, in a room of its own. Expo, short for expediter, stands at the pass and calls the line, and has an entry of its own. A small kitchen may fold three of these stations into one cook.

Brennan's menus show how much fry work one kitchen can carry. The house lists popcorn shrimp, fried Gulf shrimp, fried pickles, crispy artichokes and a fried Cornish hen among its fried dishes, and its guide sends every question about coatings, shared fryers or the oil to the kitchen, every time. For fish, the guide's habit is to know today's Gulf fish and how it is cooked, confirmed at lineup, the short meeting before service.

For a server, the stations explain the kitchen's rhythm. A table's plates leave together only when every station on the ticket is ready, so one late table usually means one station is behind: a grill full of steaks, a fryer coming back to heat. Ask the pass, not the cook, and give the guest a plain answer about the wait.

brennans.how: Popcorn shrimp are fry station work: classically dredged in seasoned flour or a light batter and fried quickly until golden. Every question about the coating, a shared fryer or the oil goes to the kitchen.
Sautéing is the saucier's craft: the children's Sautéed Gulf Fish is cooked quickly in a little hot fat in a wide pan and turned once. Know today's fish and its preparation at lineup.

entries.title: Calls on the line
entries.say: As it reads: calls on the line.
entries.summary: Calls are the short spoken words a kitchen runs on: oui chef, heard, behind, hot, fire, all day, eighty-six. Each says one thing fast and each is answered, so orders are heard and bodies and blades stay out of harm.
entries.guest: I'm sorry, the kitchen has just run out of that dish tonight. May I suggest something close to it?

paras: A kitchen in service is loud, hot and fast, and nobody has time for a full sentence. Calls are the short, fixed words that carry the essentials: an order heard, a body moving behind you, a pan too hot to touch, a dish run out. Every cook learns the same words, so they mean the same thing in every mouth, and every call is answered. As far as the kitchen knows, a call that is not answered was not heard.

Oui, chef, or yes, chef, is the answer to an instruction from the chef or the pass, the counter where finished plates leave the kitchen. It does not mean agreement; it means I heard it and I am on it. Heard does the same job in many American kitchens: the expediter, who runs the pass, calls an order and the station answers heard. In a French kitchen a new order may be announced with ça marche (sah MARSH), literally it walks: it is going, start it. Cooks say it back to mean got it, it's going.

Fire means cook it now: fire table twelve tells each station to start that table's next course. Ordering, in many kitchens, reads a new ticket aloud so stations can get ready before the fire. All day is the running total across every open ticket: four filets all day means four to cook in all. On the fly means as fast as possible, ahead of the queue, usually for a missed or dropped plate. Walking in warns that a party or a large order has just arrived. In the window means plates are up at the pass, waiting to go. Hands, called from the pass, means plates are ready and someone must carry them now.

Eighty-six means out: eighty-six the soup means no more soup tonight. The cook calls it to the pass the moment the last portion goes, and the servers must hear it before they sell another. Where the phrase came from is disputed, and no single story is proven. In the weeds means a station is overwhelmed and falling behind. Saying so early is a strength, not a confession: help can be sent only to a cook who asks.

Some calls exist, by long kitchen custom, to prevent injuries. Behind means someone is passing at your back: hold still, and do not step back or turn suddenly. Corner warns that someone is coming round a blind corner. Hot means a hot pan, tray or pot is moving: give way, and never grab what has just been set down. Sharp means a knife is being carried, point down and close to the leg. Call loudly, every time, even in a quiet kitchen: the habit works only if it never lapses.

The common failures are silence and assumption. A cook who does not answer leaves the pass guessing, so the call comes again, louder, while the table waits. A cook who moves without calling behind or hot invites a burn or a spill. A server who sells a dish after it has been eighty-sixed promises the guest something the kitchen cannot make. The fix is always the same: call it, answer it, and repeat the essential part back, so fire table twelve is met with heard, twelve.

Servers hear these calls too and answer them like cooks. When the kitchen eighty-sixes a dish, it comes off the server's list at once, and the guest hears it in plain English, never kitchen slang: the kitchen has run out of that tonight, and here is something close. Hands from the pass means go now if your hands are free, and a server crossing the kitchen calls behind and hot like everyone else.

faults.cause: The cook did not hear it, or heard it and stayed silent.
faults.fix: Answer every call with heard or oui, chef, and repeat the table or the item back.

faults.fault: A collision or a burn at someone's back
faults.cause: A cook moved behind another, or carried a hot pan, without calling.
faults.fix: Call behind, hot or sharp loudly every time, even in a quiet kitchen.

faults.fault: A dish sold after it has run out
faults.cause: The eighty-six never reached the floor, or a server missed it.
faults.fix: Call it to the pass the moment the last portion goes; every server strikes it at once.

faults.cause: A cook too proud or too busy to say in the weeds.
faults.fix: Say it early, so the sous chef can send help before the tickets pile up.

entries.title: The pass and expediting
entries.say: As it reads: the pass and expediting.
entries.summary: The pass is the counter between kitchen and dining room where every plate is checked before it goes. The expediter runs it, reading tickets, firing courses and timing each table so its plates leave together, hot and right.
entries.guest: The pass is where the kitchen checks each plate before it comes out, so a table's dishes can arrive together, as the cooks mean them to be.

paras: The pass is the counter, often under heat lamps, between the hot line and the dining room. Cooks set finished plates on one side and servers collect them from the other. It is the kitchen's last checkpoint: nothing reaches a guest without crossing it, so whoever stands there sees every plate the kitchen sends. In the classical brigade the aboyeur called the orders there, with the chef or the sous chef beside him checking the plates; in many American kitchens the expediter, called expo, does both jobs.

The expediter, the aboyeur of the old brigade, owns the tickets. As each order arrives the expediter reads it to the line so the stations can prepare, then fires each course when the table is ready for it: soup bowls cleared, fire the mains. Plates are called for by table, collected as they come up and checked one by one against the ticket: the right dish, cooked as ordered, with its sauce and garnish, hot, with a clean rim and nothing missing.

Timing is the craft. A table's plates should leave together, so the expediter counts back from the slowest dish: if the steak takes twelve minutes with its rest and the fish six, the steak is fired first and the fish six minutes later, and both reach the pass at the same moment. Hot food goes out hot, on warm plates. A sauce that has sat long enough to form a skin goes back for fresh, because a plate that dies under the lamp reaches the guest worse.

A server at the pass has one job: carry the plates as they leave, quickly and correctly. Arrive with hands free, know the table and its seat numbers so each guest gets their plate without being asked who had the fish, and hold each plate from underneath, the thumb flat on the outer edge of the rim and pointing outwards, never across the rim the cook has just wiped or near the food. Check the ticket as you lift. If a table is not ready, a guest away or menus still open, tell the expediter before the course is fired, not after.

A refire is a dish cooked again, and a remake one rebuilt, usually because it came back from the table or failed the check: a steak over or under, a cold plate, the wrong order. Bring a problem to the pass calmly and plainly: table, seat, dish, what is wrong and what the guest would like. The expediter fires the replacement first, ahead of the queue, and decides whether the rest of the table waits or eats. Blame waits until after service; the guest's dinner cannot.

A plate for a guest with an allergy is handled differently by the kitchen from the moment the ticket is written. The server writes the need on the ticket the way the house requires, and the kitchen decides what the dish can be. At the pass that allergy plate is flagged, checked against the ticket with the kitchen and carried separately: alone, never stacked with other plates or handed to whoever is free, straight to its seat. The full conversation with the guest has its own entry; at the pass, every allergy question goes to the kitchen.

At Brennan's the house guide is plain: guests note dietary needs at the reservation, the server writes them on the ticket, and the kitchen clears every choice, because the kitchen, not the server, says what a dish can do. Its practice scenarios add: flag the ticket and tell the captain.

entries.title: Menu French a server says
entries.summary: The few dozen French words an American menu still carries: the little joining words, the course names, the ways a meal is priced, and the sauce and cooking words guests ask about. Say each simply, then in plain English.
entries.guest: En papillote just means in paper: the fish is sealed in a parcel, here a banana leaf, so it steams in its own juices and stays moist.

paras: Menu French is the small set of French words American menus still use: joining words, course names, ways of pricing a meal, and the sauce and cooking words guests ask about. You need no French, just a few dozen words said clearly, with the plain meaning ready behind each.

The little words tell you how to read the rest. À la (ah LAH) means in the style of: à la Créole is the Creole way. Au and aux (both OH) mean with: au jus is with its juice. En (AHN) means in: en croûte, in pastry. Sur (SOOR) means on, and de (DUH) means of: pot de crème, literally a pot of cream, is a baked custard set in a little pot. In a long name the main ingredient usually comes first, and the little word says what comes with it or how it is cooked.

The course words follow the meal. An amuse-bouche (ah-mooz BOOSH), a mouth amuser, is one bite the chef sends before the meal, neither ordered nor charged. Hors d'oeuvre (or DURV), literally outside the work, means small savoury bites served apart from the meal. Entrée (AHN-tray) is the trap. In nineteenth-century French dinners it was a substantial dish served before the roast; American menus kept it for the main course, while in France today it means the starter, and the main is the plat (PLAH). Dessert is the same word in both, and mignardises (meen-yar-DEEZ) are the small sweets served with coffee.

À la carte (ah lah KART) means from the card: every dish chosen and priced on its own. Prix fixe (pree FEEKS) means fixed price: a set run of courses for one price, often with a choice at each. Table d'hôte (tah-bluh DOHT), the host's table, began as an inn's meal at a set hour and price, and now means much the same. A tasting menu, dégustation (day-goos-tah-SYOHN), is a longer run of small courses chosen by the kitchen.

Jus (ZHOO) is the natural juice of a roast, often reduced, thinner than a sauce. A coulis (koo-LEE) is a smooth, sieved purée of fruit or vegetables used as a sauce, and a purée is anything blended smooth. A mousse is lightened with whipped cream or beaten egg white, sweet or savoury. Velouté (veh-loo-TAY), velvety, is a light stock of veal, chicken or fish thickened with a blond roux, and on many menus a smooth, creamy soup. Beurre (BURR) is butter and crème (KREM) is cream.

Confit (kohn-FEE), from the French for to preserve, is food cooked slowly in fat or syrup: classically duck legs cured with salt and cooked under fat until tender, then crisped; garlic or tomato confit is cooked slowly in oil, and fruit confit is preserved in sugar. Flambé (flahm-BAY) means flamed: spirit lit in a hot pan. En papillote (ahn pah-pee-YOHT) means sealed in a parcel and baked, so the food steams in its own juices. Meunière (muhn-YAIR), the miller's wife's way, is fish dusted in flour, cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley.

The common slips are easy to hear: jus said like juice, the h or s of hors sounded, with au jus, which says with twice, and entrée used without saying which end of the meal you mean. One habit mends them all: say the word once, then say what it is.

At Brennan's the entrées are main courses, listed after the starters, soups and salads. The Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper; ask at lineup, the short meeting before service, whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest of the steam. The two $80 tasting menus of the eightieth year are prix fixe: a set run of courses at one price. The Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit, and Bananas Foster is flambéed on the guéridon (gay-ree-DOHN), the tableside cart.

Lead with the dish and let the French follow: the duck confit, a leg cooked slowly in duck fat until tender, then crisped. Never correct how a guest says a word; use your own way in your next sentence. When you do not know a word, ask the kitchen: a server who checks is trusted, and one who guesses is not.

faults.cause: Reading a French word as English, so jus becomes juice and the s of hors is said.
faults.fix: Learn the few dozen words aloud before service, with their respellings, and say them plainly.

faults.cause: Au already means with, so the phrase says with twice.
faults.fix: Say served au jus, or with its juice.

faults.cause: In France the word means a starter; on an American menu, a main course.
faults.fix: Say main course or starter as well, so the guest knows which end of the meal you mean.

faults.cause: The word was said and never explained.
faults.fix: Say the word once, then say what it is in plain English.

brennans.how: The Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, so the fish steams in its own juices. Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest about the steam.
The Rohan duck leg on the Duck Confit Waffle is confit: cured, cooked slowly under fat, then crisped. Describe the method in general and promise no house times.
Bananas Foster is flambéed at the table on the guéridon, the tableside cart: the spirit is lit in the pan and the flame dies before the dessert is plated.

The Traditional Breakfast, one of the two $80 tasting menus of the eightieth year, is a prix fixe: a set run of courses at one price, with the Eggs Hussarde among its courses. Read its pours from the printed card at lineup.

entries.title: Mise en place words
entries.summary: The French names a classical kitchen uses for its pans, strainers, herb bundles, prep jobs and flavour bases. Read at sight, they turn a prep list into clear work: monder the tomatoes, a bouquet garni for the stock, duxelles for the filling.
entries.guest: Persillade is a fresh topping of chopped parsley and garlic; on our Creole Hanger Steak it comes with toasted pumpkin seeds for crunch.

paras: Mise en place (meez ahn PLAHS), everything in its place, is the cook's setting up before service, and it has an entry of its own; this one is its vocabulary. A classical kitchen names its pans, strainers, herb bundles, prep jobs and flavour bases in French, in short words made for speed. A sous chef writes the prep list in them and expects every cook to read it at sight.

Vessels first. A bain-marie (ban mah-REE) is a water bath for gentle heat, and also the tall steel pot that holds a sauce in it on the line. A sautoir (soh-TWAHR) is a straight-sided sauté pan that keeps a pan sauce in; a sauteuse (soh-TUHZ) has sloping sides for tossing and fast reduction. A rondeau (rohn-DOH) is wide and fairly shallow with two loop handles, for braising in quantity. A marmite (mar-MEET) is a tall lidded stockpot, a russe (ROOS) a long-handled saucepan, and a plaque (PLAHK) a flat baking tray.

Then the tools. A chinois (sheen-WAH) is a cone of fine mesh for straining sauces and stocks; American kitchens call the coarser perforated cone a china cap. A tamis (tah-MEE) is a drum sieve for pressing purées smooth. An étamine (ay-tah-MEEN) is a straining cloth of muslin or cheesecloth, for the clearest liquids. A mandoline (man-doh-LEEN) is a blade set in a frame for even slices, used with its guard every time. A spider is a wide wire skimmer for lifting food from oil or water.

Bundles carry flavour into a pot and come out again. A bouquet garni (boo-KAY gar-NEE) is parsley stalks, thyme and a bay leaf wrapped in leek green and tied, the string fastened to the handle so it lifts out. A sachet d'épices (sah-SHAY day-PEES) does the same for loose spice: peppercorns, bay, thyme and parsley stems knotted in cheesecloth. An oignon piqué (on-YOHN pee-KAY) is a peeled onion with a bay leaf pinned on by cloves, simmered in milk for béchamel, milk thickened with a roux. An oignon brûlé (on-YOHN broo-LAY) is a halved onion charred dark on the flat top, the griddle plate, for colour in brown stock and consommé, a clear soup of clarified stock.

The verbs name jobs. Monder (mohn-DAY) is to skin after a brief blanch: score a tomato, 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water, and the skin slips off. Blanchir (blahn-SHEER) is to blanch, a brief plunge into boiling water, often then into iced water. Dégorger (day-gor-ZHAY) is to draw out, soaking sweetbreads in cold water or salting cucumber. Dépouiller (day-poo-YAY) is to skim a simmering sauce. Réduire (ray-DWEER) is to reduce and passer (pah-SAY) to strain. Napper (nah-PAY) is to coat: a sauce à la nappe coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it. Monter (mohn-TAY) is to mount, whisking in cold butter or whipping whites or cream.

Mirepoix (meer-PWAH) is onion, carrot and celery, by the standard kitchen rule two parts onion to one of each other by weight; about 450 g (1 lb) flavours 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of stock, and it is strained out. For a fish fumet, a quick fish stock, or any stock or sauce that must stay ivory-pale, a white mirepoix swaps the carrot for leek and often mushroom trimmings; a classical white veal or chicken stock keeps its carrot, simply never browned.

A matignon (mah-tee-NYOHN) is an edible mirepoix, cut fine, with ham or without, stewed gently in butter and left in the dish. Duxelles (dook-SEL) is mushrooms and shallot chopped fine and cooked in butter until every drop of moisture has gone. Persillade (pair-see-YAHD) is chopped parsley and garlic, added at the last moment. Concassée (kon-ka-SAY) means roughly chopped: tomato concassée is peeled, seeded and diced.
Most slips are confusions: a sauteuse fetched for a sautoir's job spills its sauce, and a coarse cone where the list said étamine leaves a consommé cloudy.

At Brennan's, the Seafood Gumbo starts from the holy trinity, onion, celery and green bell pepper: Louisiana's mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot, softened and left in the pot like a matignon. Creamed spinach classically begins with blanchir and a hard squeeze. The dinner Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade, with toasted pumpkin seeds.

A few of these words reach a menu: persillade on our Creole Hanger Steak, and duxelles on many classical ones. A server says the word, then what it is: chopped parsley and garlic; mushrooms chopped fine and cooked down in butter.

faults.cause: A sauteuse fetched when the job needed a sautoir, whose straight sides hold liquid.
faults.fix: Learn the two by their sides: straight for a sautoir, sloping for a sauteuse.

faults.cause: Strained through a coarse cone, or pressed hard through the mesh.
faults.fix: Pass it through a fine chinois or an étamine, and let it run rather than forcing it.

faults.fix: Cook until the pan is dry and the paste pulls together, then cool it before use.

faults.fix: Count 10 to 15 seconds, then go straight into iced water.

faults.cause: A bouquet garni tied loosely, or a sachet that split.
faults.fix: Tie it tight with string, tie the end to the handle, and lift it out whole.

brennans.how: The gumbo starts from the holy trinity, onion, celery and green bell pepper softened together: Louisiana's mirepoix, with bell pepper in place of carrot. Unlike a stock's mirepoix, it is never strained out.

Creamed spinach classically begins with blanchir: blanched, plunged into iced water, squeezed hard and chopped, then bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg. Confirm the house method with the kitchen.
The Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade: the French parsley and garlic finish, thrown on at the last second, with toasted pumpkin seeds for crunch.

cards.back: Mirepoix is rough-cut onion, carrot and celery, two to one to one, strained out; matignon is cut fine, stewed in butter and left in the dish.

cards.front: What are duxelles and persillade?
cards.back: Duxelles: mushrooms and shallot chopped fine, cooked in butter until every drop of moisture has gone and the paste pulls together. Persillade: chopped parsley and garlic, added at the last moment.

questions.q: The sous chef calls for a sautoir to finish a pan sauce. What do you bring?
questions.answer: A straight-sided sauté pan
questions.why: A sautoir's straight sides hold a pan sauce; the sloping sauteuse is for tossing, the rondeau braises in quantity and the marmite makes stock.

questions.q: Which of these strains a consommé clearest?
questions.answer: An étamine
questions.why: An étamine is a cloth of muslin or cheesecloth, finer than any mesh, so it holds back what a cone, a drum sieve or a colander lets through.

questions.q: Why is a bouquet garni tied with string, the end fastened to the handle?
questions.answer: So it lifts out whole once its flavour is in
distractors: So it holds the herbs below the surface
So the leek green cooks evenly with it
So the cook can tell when it is done
questions.why: The bundle carries flavour into the pot and must come out again; tied and fastened, it leaves no loose herbs to strain out.

questions.q: Which bundle is the classical one for the milk of a béchamel?
questions.answer: An oignon piqué
questions.why: The oignon piqué, an onion with a bay leaf pinned on by cloves, is simmered in the milk; the brûlé colours brown stock, and the bouquet and sachet flavour stocks and braises.

questions.q: A prep list says monder the tomatoes. What do you do?
questions.answer: Blanch them briefly and slip off the skins
distractors: Roast them in a hot oven until they collapse
Salt them to draw out their water
Chop them roughly with their skins on
questions.why: Monder is to skin after a brief blanch: 10 to 15 seconds in boiling water, then iced water, and the skin slips off.

questions.q: What is a cook doing when told to dépouiller the sauce?
questions.answer: Skimming fat and scum from its surface
distractors: Whisking cold butter into it off the heat
Coating the plate with it before service
Straining it through a cloth into a pan
questions.why: Dépouiller is skimming; mounting with butter is monter, coating is napper and straining is passer.

questions.q: How do you know a sauce has reached nappe?
questions.answer: It coats a spoon and holds a line drawn through it
distractors: It sets firm in the fridge when it is chilled overnight
It runs straight off the spoon like water
It forms stiff peaks when it is whisked hard
questions.why: Napper means to coat: a sauce at nappe clings to the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line.

questions.q: What is the standard proportion of a mirepoix by weight?
questions.answer: Two parts onion, one carrot, one celery
distractors: Equal parts onion, carrot and celery
Two parts carrot, one onion, one leek
Two parts celery, one onion, one carrot
questions.why: Onion leads at half the weight, with carrot and celery a quarter each; the mix is cut to suit the cooking time and strained out.

questions.q: Duxelles for a pastry filling is taken off the heat too soon. What goes wrong?
questions.answer: The wet paste makes the pastry soggy
distractors: The mushrooms turn bitter and black
The shallot stays raw and sharp
The butter sets hard in the filling
questions.why: Duxelles is cooked until every drop of moisture has gone; any water left behind soaks into the pastry around it.

questions.q: Our dinner Creole Hanger Steak carries a pepita persillade. What is a persillade?
questions.answer: Chopped parsley and garlic, added at the end
distractors: Mushrooms and shallot cooked dry in butter
Onion, carrot and celery cut fine
questions.why: Persillade, from persil, parsley, is chopped parsley and garlic thrown on at the last moment; duxelles is the mushroom paste, concassée the tomato and matignon the fine-cut vegetables.

entries.title: The cuts by name
entries.say: As it reads: the cuts by name.
entries.summary: The French names for the classical cuts: strips, dice, slices and shapes, from julienne to tourné, and the garnish names that promise a cut. Each name is a promise of shape, on a prep list and on a menu.
entries.guest: Our Brabant potatoes are cubed and fried golden, then tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; a pavé is thin potato layers pressed into a neat brick and seared.

paras: Each classical cut carries a French name, and the name is a promise of shape. Julienne means fine strips, brunoise tiny dice, tourné a seven-sided barrel. A prep list written in these names tells a cook exactly what to cut, and a menu that uses them tells a guest what will be on the plate. This entry is the vocabulary, what each name means and how to say it; the knife work and the exact measures belong to Knife cuts.

The strips run from fine to thick. Julienne (zhoo-lee-EN) is the finest, a thin matchstick that cooks in moments or sits raw in a salad. Allumette (ah-loo-MET), a match, is about the size of julienne or a touch thicker, and mostly a potato word, for fries cut thin. Bâtonnet (bah-toh-NAY), a little stick, is thicker and square, the strip a cook cuts on the way to a dice. Pont-neuf (pohn NUHF) is the thick potato stick fried as a chunky chip, often stacked like logs.

A dice is a strip cut across into cubes, so each strip has its dice. Julienne cut across gives brunoise (broon-WAHZ), the finest dice, for the end of a sauce or to garnish a consommé, a clear soup. Bâtonnet gives macédoine (mah-say-DWAHN), a small, even dice. A thicker stick gives parmentier (par-mahn-TYAY), a larger cube, classically of potato. Mirepoix (meer-PWAH) is the exception: a rough cut, sized to how long it will cook and strained out at the end, so nobody cuts it to an exact size.

Paysanne (pay-ee-ZAHN), country style, is thin, flat pieces that keep the outline of the vegetable, squares, rounds or triangles, for soup. A rondelle (rohn-DEL) is a round cut straight across a carrot or cucumber. Émincé (ay-man-SAY) means thinly sliced; on a menu, an émincé is thin strips of meat. A chiffonade (shif-uh-NAHD) is leaves rolled and sliced into fine ribbons. Ciseler (seez-LAY) is to chop an onion or shallot very fine, slicing one way and then across, so it falls into tiny even pieces without being crushed. A tourné (toor-NAY), turned, is a barrel with seven faces and flat ends. Parisienne (pah-ree-ZYEN) means balls scooped with a melon baller.

Some garnish names promise a cut. Jardinière (zhar-dee-NYAIR), from the garden, means vegetables in bâtonnets, carrots and turnips with peas and French beans. Printanière (pran-tah-NYAIR), spring, means young vegetables cut small or turned at the start of their season. Macédoine is both a cut and a dish: a mix of diced vegetables, or of fruit, cut to that small dice.

Two names honour a man and a bridge. Parmentier is Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the pharmacist who campaigned for the potato in eighteenth-century France, which is why his name means potato on a menu. Pont-neuf is usually linked to the Pont Neuf in Paris, where street sellers are said to have fried potatoes. Where julienne came from, nobody has proved.

On the line, the name means the house size: a chef who asks for brunoise shallots means the brunoise this kitchen cuts, so if you are unsure, cut a few and show them before you cut the lot. On the floor, say the name and then the shape in plain words: a julienne of vegetables is fine matchsticks, a chiffonade of basil is fine ribbons, pommes parisiennes are little potato balls.

On the Brennan's menus the potatoes carry the lesson. Brabant potatoes are cubed, blanched or par-fried, then fried golden and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup, the short meeting before service. The smoked potato pavé on the Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is named for its shape: pavé is French for paving stone, and a pavé is classically potato sliced paper-thin, layered, pressed, cut into bricks and seared; the house's own method is the kitchen's detail.

faults.cause: A plain dice cut where the list said brunoise.
faults.fix: Read the name as a shape and size; when unsure, cut a few and show the chef first.

faults.cause: Paysanne cut thick or in pieces of different sizes.
faults.fix: Keep paysanne thin and even, following the outline of the vegetable.

faults.fault: A chiffonade blackened at the edges
faults.cause: Cut long before service, or with a dull knife that bruises the leaves.
faults.fix: Cut it with a sharp knife at the last moment.

faults.fault: A cloudy stock full of shreds
faults.cause: Mirepoix cut fine for a stock that simmers for hours.
faults.fix: Size the mirepoix to the cooking time: large for a long stock, small for a quick sauce.

brennans.how: Brabant potatoes are cubed, blanched or par-fried, then fried golden and crisp and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley. Confirm the house finish and fryer at lineup.

Pavé means paving stone, for its neat rectangular block of thin potato layers, cut into bricks and seared until each face is crisp. The house method, and where the smoke comes in, are the kitchen's detail.

Rough chunks sized for a long stock

questions.q: As a cut, what is parmentier?

Thin, flat pieces that keep the outline

questions.q: A dish is served with a jardinière garnish. What cut should the vegetables be?
questions.answer: Bâtonnets
questions.why: Jardinière, from the garden, promises vegetables cut in bâtonnets, usually carrots and turnips with peas and French beans.

questions.q: Why is a mirepoix for a long stock cut large?
questions.answer: It must last the cooking without breaking down
distractors: It must look neat and even on the finished plate
It must soften fully within a minute or two
It must pass through the chinois with the stock
questions.why: Mirepoix is sized to its cooking time and strained out; cut fine for a long simmer it breaks down and clouds the stock.

entries.title: Cooking terms on the ticket
entries.say: As it reads: cooking terms on the ticket.
entries.summary: The words that carry an order from the table to the kitchen: doneness in French and English, egg orders, modifiers such as no, add, sub and on the side, seat numbers, and an allergy written down and said to the kitchen.
entries.guest: How would you like the filet cooked? Medium rare has a warm red centre; medium is pink in the centre, with a little less juice.

paras: A ticket is the order as the kitchen reads it: each dish, how it is cooked, what changes and which seat it goes to. Its words are short and fixed, so nothing is misread. Write it well and the kitchen has everything at once; write it badly and back comes a steak or a plate nobody can place.

Doneness, called temperature on the floor, is the first thing a ticket carries for meat. French kitchens use four words. Bleu (BLUH) is seared hard outside and barely warmed within. Saignant (sen-YAHN), bleeding, is rare: red and juicy at the centre. À point (ah PWAN), at the point, is pink through, roughly medium rare to medium. Bien cuit (byan KWEE) is well done. American kitchens use five steps, rare, medium rare, medium, medium well and well done. Roughly, at the centre after resting: rare about 52°C (126°F), medium rare 57°C (135°F), medium 60 to 63°C (140 to 145°F), medium well 65°C (149°F), well done 71°C (160°F) or more.

The two ladders do not line up. The French count four steps to the American five, so à point covers what an American kitchen splits into medium rare and medium, and French cooking leans rarer: a guest who says à point may mean either. Translate by colour, not by word: ask what the guest wants to see at the centre, red, pink or none, and write the house word for it. Each kitchen sets its own marks. The USDA recommends 63°C (145°F) and a three-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, and menus that serve meat less cooked print a consumer advisory, as the FDA Food Code asks.

Egg orders name what the guest will see. Poached is cooked out of the shell in water, white set and yolk running. Sunny side up is fried on one side only, never turned, the yolk liquid. Over easy is fried and turned briefly, the yolk still runny; over medium and over hard cook it further. Soft-boiled is simmered in the shell so the yolk stays soft. Soft scrambled is stirred gently into moist, creamy curds. How each is cooked belongs to the egg station; the ticket's job is to say which, exactly.

Modifiers change a dish. On the side means a sauce or dressing served apart. No takes something off; add puts something on, often at a charge; sub swaps one thing for another, only when the kitchen allows it. Rush means the table needs it fast, and VIP marks a guest the house wants looked after with extra care. Hold means wait until fire, which means cook it now; since some kitchens also use hold for leave off, write no for anything taken away. À la minute (ah lah mee-NOOT) means cooked to order at that moment, against made ahead, prepared earlier and finished to order.

Seat numbers place each plate. Every table has a seat one, fixed by house rule from a landmark such as the door or the window, and the rest follow round the table in one direction. Each order is written against its seat, so the runner can set every plate before the right guest without asking who had what.

An allergy goes on the ticket and to the kitchen by voice, every time. Write it as the system flags it, then tell the chef or the expediter, and the captain, in person. The ticket carries the order through service; the spoken word makes sure a person has heard it. The kitchen, not the server, decides what a dish can do, so promise nothing until it has cleared the order.

At Brennan's the filet on the Traditional Breakfast has its temperature taken with the order. The poached eggs on the Eggs Hussarde come soft unless the guest asks otherwise; check with the kitchen before promising firmer eggs. Egg Any Style is one egg in the guest's style, written exactly; confirm the styles offered at lineup, the short meeting before service. Whether the Chateaubriand for two can go out at two temperatures is a lineup question, not a promise. Restrictions are noted at the reservation, written on the ticket and cleared by the kitchen.

entries.title: The old French dish names
entries.say: As it reads: the old French dish names.
entries.summary: Classical French cooking names dishes for garnishes, regions and people, and each name promises what is on the plate: Clamart means peas, Argenteuil asparagus, Rossini foie gras and truffle. New Orleans added names of its own.
entries.guest: Florentine on a French menu means the dish comes with spinach, and Véronique means grapes: the old names tell you what is on the plate before the description does.

paras: Classical French cooking names dishes after places, people and the things that come with them, and every name is a promise: Clamart means peas before the description says so. For a Chef these names are the old kitchen's working vocabulary; for a server they answer a guest's commonest question: what does that mean?

Read a name in three parts. The main item comes first: sole, poulet (chicken), oeufs (eggs) or tournedos (TOOR-nuh-doh), a small round steak from the fillet. Then the link, à la, often dropped, so tournedos à la Rossini becomes tournedos Rossini. À la is short for à la mode de, in the fashion of, which is why the name after it is feminine: à la bourguignonne. Last comes the name, pointing to a garnish, a region or a person. Decide which, and you have read the plate.

Garnish names come from towns that grew a vegetable, or people tied to it. Florentine means spinach, after Florence, classically under a cheese sauce browned under the grill. Dubarry (doo-bah-REE) means cauliflower, for Madame du Barry, mistress of Louis XV. Clamart (klah-MAR) means peas and Argenteuil (ar-zhahn-TOY) asparagus, after two towns near Paris that grew them. Crécy (kray-SEE) means carrots, so potage Crécy is carrot soup. Parmentier means potato, for Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the pharmacist who championed it in eighteenth-century France. Véronique means grapes, after Sole Véronique, poached sole with peeled green grapes.

Style names point to a region and its larder. Bourguignonne (boor-geen-YUN), Burgundy style, means red wine, lardons (small batons of bacon), mushrooms and small glazed onions; in boeuf bourguignon the word turns masculine to agree with boeuf. Lyonnaise means onions cooked golden in butter. Provençale means tomato, garlic and olive oil. Normande means Normandy's cream, and on many menus its apples or cider. Forestière, from the forest, means mushrooms. Grenobloise (greh-noh-BLWAHZ) means capers and lemon, usually with brown butter and croutons, on fish.

Names for people flatter a patron or a star. Rossini (roh-SEE-nee), for the composer Gioachino Rossini, means foie gras, fattened duck or goose liver, and truffle: tournedos Rossini sits on a fried crouton under a slice of each, with a Madeira sauce. Soubise (soo-BEEZ), for the Prince de Soubise, a marshal of France under Louis XV, means a purée of onions. Mornay means coated in a cheese sauce and browned, though whose name it carries is disputed. Chateaubriand (shah-toh-bree-AHN), for the writer and statesman François-René de Chateaubriand, is a thick cut from the centre of the fillet.

New Orleans kept the habit. Hussarde, hussar style, means poached eggs on Canadian bacon over a toasted base, with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, beneath and hollandaise on top; a recipe was printed in 1895, credited to a New York hotel chef, and Brennan's made it famous from about 1950. Sardou, named at Antoine's for the playwright Victorien Sardou, began as poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, finished with ham, anchovy and truffle; most later versions dropped those for creamed spinach. Rockefeller, also Antoine's, means oysters baked under a rich green sauce, named for John D. Rockefeller for its richness.

Bienville, for the city's founder, means oysters under a shrimp and mushroom cream sauce, most often credited to Arnaud's, though Antoine's has claimed it too. Pontchartrain names the lake north of the city, itself named for a minister of Louis XIV; on menus it often means fish topped with crabmeat. Clemenceau, for Georges Clemenceau, who led France at the end of the First World War, means chicken with fried potatoes, mushrooms, peas and garlic, most often credited to Galatoire's.

Some names have drifted, and a Chef knows both meanings. Eggs Florentine on an American brunch menu is usually a Benedict with spinach in place of the ham. Classical sole normande came with oysters, mussels, shrimp and mushrooms under sauce normande, a fish velouté (fish stock thickened with a blond roux) enriched with egg yolks and cream, and no apples. Chateaubriand was a thick grilled steak; many menus now roast the centre cut whole for two. Most copies of Oysters Rockefeller use spinach, though Antoine's has said its own sauce holds none. The house decides what its name means, so read its description too.

At the table, say the name, then what it means in plain English: “Florentine means it comes on spinach.” Never use a name to show off, and never correct a guest who says it differently. Unsure how the house makes a named dish? Ask the kitchen rather than promise the classic.

entries.title: Say it: the Brennan's menu
entries.say: As it reads: say it, the Brennan's menu.
entries.summary: The house's say-it list: the French and Louisiana words a server says most on the Brennan's menu, each with the house guide's respelling, from hollandaise and Hussarde to roux and pralines, and the habit of saying each name, then what it is.
entries.guest: Our Eggs Hussarde, hussar style, is poached eggs on Canadian bacon with a red wine sauce beneath and hollandaise on top: New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict.

paras: This is the say-it list for our menu: the French and Louisiana words a new server or cook says every shift, with the house guide's respellings. A respelling writes the word the way an American dining room says it, with the stressed syllable in capitals: bair-NAYZ. A name said cleanly tells a guest you know the plate; a name stumbled over makes them doubt the rest. One habit goes with every name: say it, then say what it is in plain English.

Start with the sauces, because they name most of the plates. Hollandaise, HOL-un-dayz, is the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce of Eggs Benedict. Béarnaise, bair-NAYZ, is hollandaise's cousin: egg yolk and butter sharpened with a reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon, the classic sauce for steak. Choron, sho-ROHN, is béarnaise with tomato. Foyot, fwah-YO, is béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. Marchand de vin, mar-SHAHN duh VAN, the wine merchant's sauce, is a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce; whether tonight's carries mushroom or ham is a question for the chef. Beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, is a silky white wine and butter sauce, with no K sound at the end.

Then the dishes. Hussarde, hoo-SARD, means hussar style. Sardou, sar-DOO, carries the name of a French playwright. Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, means with grapes. En papillote, ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means in paper, though our Gulf Fish en Papillote is wrapped in banana leaf. Poussin, poo-SAN, means young chicken: our Poussin à la Moutarde uses a Cornish hen, the nearest American bird, brined in sweet tea, fried and sauced with mustard cream. Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the thick centre cut of the beef tenderloin, roasted for two.

The Louisiana words come next. Roux, ROO, is flour cooked in fat and stirred, white or blond for French sauces and taken to a dark brown for gumbo and turtle soup; the darker it goes, the more flavour and the less thickening, and how dark ours goes is a question for the chef. Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, is the smoky Louisiana pork sausage in our gumbo; tell a guest who avoids pork that it is in the gumbo before they order. Tasso, TAH-so, is Cajun spiced, cured and smoked pork that seasons the sauce of the shrimp and grits.

Guests in this city ask about étouffée, ay-too-FAY, so know it whether or not tonight's menu carries it: it means smothered, crawfish or shrimp cooked down in a thick sauce over rice. Pralines, PRAH-leen, are the pecan and brown sugar candies that add crunch to our bread pudding. Café brûlot, ka-FAY broo-LOH, is the city's spiced, flamed coffee, whose flavours our coffee cake borrows.

Four words trip people. Débris, DAY-bree, is meltingly tender slow-cooked meat in its own gravy: on the Eggs Owen, short rib braised in red wine. Brabant, bra-BAHNT, names our crisp cubed potatoes. Mignonette, min-yo-NET, is the raw bar sauce of vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper for oysters. Fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, with the S of fines carried onto herbes, is the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, on the crab claws.

Some words are said two ways; follow the house. The guide gives Hussarde as hoo-SARD, though hoo-ZARD is heard. It gives mignonette as min-yo-NET, and meen-yo-NET, nearer the French, is also heard. Tasso is TAH-so, though TASS-oh is heard too. Brabant is bra-BAHNT in the guide, bra-BAHN in French and bruh-BANT to many locals. Pralines are PRAH-leen, never PRAY-leen. Which the floor uses for Hussarde, tasso and Brabant is a question for the manager at lineup, the short meeting before service. Until then, use the guide's respelling, and never correct a guest.

Three names carry a story the house wants told with care. Eggs Hussarde is our signature, but the dish is older than the restaurant, so never say it was invented here. Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style, with crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron. Redfish Véronique keeps the grapes of the French classic and pickles them in hibiscus.

At the table, say the name once, clearly, then the plain English: “The Sardou, sar-DOO, is poached eggs over crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach, with a tomato béarnaise.” Never use the French to show off, and never make a guest feel wrong for saying it differently. If a guest asks what goes into a sauce, give the description, and send any allergy question to the kitchen.

faults.cause: Reading the French spelling as if it were English.
faults.fix: Say burr BLAHN: the final C is silent, as the house notes.

faults.cause: The pronunciation common outside New Orleans.
faults.fix: Say PRAH-leen, the house habit, never PRAY-leen.

faults.fix: Say it the house way yourself and let the guest's version stand.

brennans.how: Say hoo-SARD, then: poached eggs on Canadian bacon with marchand de vin beneath and hollandaise on top, New Orleans' answer to Eggs Benedict. Call it our signature, never invented here.

Say sar-DOO, then: poached eggs with crispy artichokes, Parmesan creamed spinach and Choron. Created at Antoine's and named for the playwright Victorien Sardou; ours is Antoine's dish in the Brennan's style.
Say vay-ro-NEEK, then: with grapes. Our Redfish Véronique carries hibiscus-pickled grapes and a preserved lemon beurre blanc in place of the classic's fresh grapes and creamy sauce.
Say fwah-YO, then: béarnaise made even richer with a reduced beef glaze. On the Roasted Chateaubriand it brings the depth that the lean tenderloin lacks.
The guide prints bra-BAHNT; the French say bra-BAHN and many locals bruh-BANT, so confirm the floor's habit at lineup. Then: crisp fried potato cubes, a New Orleans classic.
Say min-yo-NET, then: shallot and cracked pepper in vinegar. Ours carries preserved Fresno chilli and parsley on the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, spooned on by the guest at the table.
